issues.legal_issue: The preventive-detention statute was constitutionally valid because it was enacted within legislative competence and received presidential assent.
material_facts: The statute concerned preventive detention and was enacted under the relevant Concurrent List entry.
The statute was reserved for the President’s consideration and received presidential assent.
issues.legal_principle: The State legislature could enact the statute under Entry 3 of List III of the Seventh Schedule, and presidential assent supported its validity.

predicates.preventive_detention_law: The law provides for detention to prevent activities considered prejudicial to public order.
predicates.law_within_concurrent_legislative_compet: The law concerns a subject assigned to the concurrent legislative field.
predicates.presidential_assent_received: The law was reserved for and received the President’s assent.

issues.definition: When a preventive-detention law falls within concurrent legislative competence and receives presidential assent, the law is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A State Government may delegate preventive-detention powers to locally responsible officials where local conditions make their prompt exercise necessary.
material_facts: The State Government had delegated detention powers to District Magistrates and Commissioners of Police in specified areas.
The delegation was based on circumstances prevailing or likely to prevail in those areas and the officials were responsible for maintaining public order there.
The challenged delegation had not been periodically reviewed after it was made.
issues.conclusion: The delegation was valid, and periodic review was not required so long as the relevant activities and need for local action persisted.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(1) and (2) of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Act, 1985, the State Government may authorize specified officials to exercise detention powers. The Court distinguished A.K. Roy v. Union of India, AIR 1982 SC 710, in light of the statutory and factual context, including the need for prompt local action.

rule.if: preventive_detention_proceeding and state_authorized_local_officials and local_public_order_risk_persisted and officials_responsible_for_local_public_order

predicates.preventive_detention_proceeding: The proceeding concerns preventive detention under a law that permits the State Government to authorize local officials to act.
predicates.state_authorized_local_officials: The State Government authorized local officials to exercise detention powers within defined areas.
predicates.local_public_order_risk_persisted: The relevant anti-social activities and risk to public order persisted in the areas covered by the authorization.
predicates.officials_responsible_for_local_public_o: The authorized officials were directly responsible for maintaining public order in those areas.

issues.definition: A delegation of preventive-detention powers is valid when the State Government authorizes locally responsible officials to respond to a continuing local public-order risk.

issues.legal_issue: Land grabbing and dealing in unlawfully occupied land or unauthorized structures may support preventive detention when the conduct adversely affects or is likely to affect public order.
material_facts: The land was found to belong to the Government, and the mutation in the partnership’s name was found to have been obtained fraudulently.
Despite an order requiring the land’s status quo to be maintained, the appellants sold much of it to third parties and purchasers made unauthorized constructions.
The purchasers became alarmed after learning of the lack of title, and the activities created tension and a feeling of insecurity in the area.
The detaining authority considered detailed material and recorded specific grounds for its satisfaction that the activities affected or were likely to affect public order.
issues.conclusion: The appellants’ activities constituted property grabbing and could justify detention to maintain public order; the Court would not re-adjudicate the authority’s subjective satisfaction where it rested on sufficient material and definite, specific grounds.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(h) and 2(i) define property grabbing and unauthorized structures, while section 3(1) and (4), including its explanation, permit detention where the relevant activities adversely affect or are likely to affect public order. The Court relied on the statutory purpose of preventing land-grabbing activities from disturbing public order and applied the limited review of subjective satisfaction where sufficient material supports specific grounds.

predicates.preventive_detention_proceeding: The case concerns an order detaining a person preventively because of alleged land-grabbing activity.
predicates.property_grabbing_or_unauthorized_dealin: The person illegally occupied land, dealt in such land or unauthorized structures, or otherwise participated in the conduct treated as property grabbing.
predicates.public_insecurity_or_alarm: The conduct caused or was likely to cause alarm, insecurity, tension, or disturbance to the public in the affected area.
predicates.specific_sufficient_material_supports_sa: The detaining authority relied on sufficient material and stated definite, specific grounds for its satisfaction about the public-order effect.

issues.definition: Detention on public-order grounds is justified when supported property-grabbing conduct causes or is likely to cause public insecurity or alarm.

issues.legal_issue: Mutation of names in revenue records does not establish title to land, and title to open land follows possession.
material_facts: The appellants relied on a partnership’s name having been entered in the revenue records to claim ownership.
The entry was found to have been procured fraudulently, and the land was treated as Government land.
The appellants transferred land despite an order requiring the status quo to be maintained.
issues.conclusion: The revenue-record mutation did not prove ownership, and the appellants could not establish that the land was their own on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Mutation entries are not evidence of title, though they may be relevant for other purposes; in respect of open land, title follows possession. The Court relied on Nirman Singh v. Rudra Patrab Narain Singh, Nageshar Baksh Singh v. Mt. Ganesha, Durga Prasad v. Ghansham Das, Ramana v. Sambamoorthy, Mohinder Singh v. State of Punjab, and Vatticherukuru Village Panchayat v. Nori Venkatarama Deekshithulu.

predicates.land_title_dispute: The case concerns competing claims to ownership of land.
predicates.ownership_claim_based_on_revenue_mutatio: A party relies on a name entered in revenue records as evidence of ownership.
predicates.no_independent_title_basis_established: The party has not established ownership by an independent basis apart from the revenue entry.

issues.definition: A revenue-record mutation alone does not establish title when a party has no independent basis for its ownership claim.

issues.legal_issue: A detention order made by an authorized official lapses unless the State Government approves it within the prescribed period, and later confirmation cannot revive it.
material_facts: The appellants’ detention orders were made by an authorized official and were executed on February 5, 1993.
The State Government’s affidavit did not establish that it approved the orders within 12 days after execution.
The Advisory Board later confirmed the orders, but the required timely approval was not shown.
issues.conclusion: The detention orders lapsed when timely State Government approval was not established, and later confirmation could not revive them.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Act, 1985 requires State Government approval within 12 days for a detention order made by an authorized official to remain in force; the Court treated that approval as mandatory. Sections 11, 12 and 13 govern reference to and consideration by the Advisory Board and confirmation, but later Board action cannot revive an order that has already lapsed.

predicates.preventive_detention_proceeding: The case concerns an order of preventive detention.
predicates.detention_order_made_by_authorized_offic: The detention order was made by an official exercising power delegated by the State Government.
predicates.state_approval_within_required_period: The State Government approved the detention order within the period required for it to remain in force.

issues.definition: An authorized official’s detention order lapses if the State Government does not approve it within the required period, and later confirmation does not restore it.

issues.legal_issue: After State Government approval of an authorized official’s detention order, only the State Government may revoke, rescind, or modify the order.
material_facts: The detention orders in the case were made by an authorized official under delegated power.
The Court considered the statutory scheme governing approval, review by the Advisory Board, and revocation of detention orders.
issues.conclusion: An authorized official may rescind an order only during its initial period of operation; after State Government approval, the State Government alone has power to revoke, rescind, or modify it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Act, 1985 governs State Government approval, section 15 gives the State Government power to revoke, rescind, or modify a detention order, and section 21 of the General Clauses Act supplies a rescission power to the authorized official only during the order’s initial operation. Article 22(5) provides the detainee’s right to make a representation.

predicates.preventive_detention_proceeding: The case concerns an order of preventive detention.
predicates.detention_order_made_by_authorized_offic: The detention order was made by an official exercising delegated power.
predicates.state_approval_given: The State Government approved the authorized official’s detention order.

issues.definition: Once an authorized official’s detention order has been approved by the State Government, only the State Government may revoke or modify it.

issues.legal_issue: The State Government must consider a detainee’s representation independently and expeditiously, rather than wait for the Advisory Board’s opinion.
material_facts: The State Government received the appellants’ representations on February 20, 1993.
It kept the representations pending while awaiting the Advisory Board’s opinion, received the Board’s report on March 23, 1993, and rejected the representations that day.
The State Government did not provide a satisfactory explanation for postponing consideration until the Board’s opinion.
issues.conclusion: Keeping the representations pending until the Advisory Board reported and considering them only afterward was unlawful and breached the constitutional requirement of expeditious consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Article 22(5) requires the Government to consider a representation independently of the Advisory Board’s consideration and to do so with reasonable speed and a sense of urgency. Any delay must be satisfactorily explained. The Court relied on Jayanarayan Sukul v. State of West Bengal, Haradhan Saha v. State of West Bengal, K.M. Abdulla Kunhi v. Union of India, and Moosa Husein Sanghar v. State of Gujarat; Article 21 protects the liberty affected by detention.

rule.if: preventive_detention_proceeding and representation_received_by_government and government_waited_for_advisory_board and not satisfactory_delay_explanation

predicates.preventive_detention_proceeding: The case concerns a person held under a preventive-detention order.
predicates.representation_received_by_government: The Government received the detainee’s representation against detention.
predicates.government_waited_for_advisory_board: The Government postponed its consideration of the representation until it received the Advisory Board’s opinion.
predicates.satisfactory_delay_explanation: The Government gave a satisfactory explanation for any delay in considering the representation.

issues.definition: Consideration of a detainee’s representation is unlawful when the Government waits for the Advisory Board and cannot satisfactorily explain the delay.
